subject: Cab Calloway — Minnie the Moocher (Blue Brothers)
editorialSubject: Cab Calloway — Minnie the Moocher (Blue Brothers)
verifiedFacts: The film The Blues Brothers was released in 1980.
Calloway performs Minnie the Moocher in the film.
John Landis pushed the performance toward a big-band arrangement rather than a disco treatment.
interestingAngle: The film did not treat Calloway as a museum piece: it rebuilt his signature number as a large, live-feeling set piece and let a new audience meet the performer inside the song.
doNotClaim: Exact performance shoot date and edit provenance are not established.
The file does not prove details beyond the sampled frames.

subject: Big Band — Rhapsody in Blue
verifiedFacts: George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue was commissioned by Paul Whiteman and premiered in 1924 with Gershwin at the piano.
Ferde Grofé orchestrated the accompaniment for the premiere and later prepared the orchestral version that became widely standard.
The work has repeatedly crossed jazz, concert, recording, and broadcast settings.
interestingAngle: Rhapsody in Blue is a work whose identity is partly its repeated rearrangement; the unknown band is not a gap to fill with a guess but part of the media object’s history.

enrichment.chartJourney: no matching relationship imposed on unidentified performance

doNotClaim: Exact orchestra, venue, program, and recording/broadcast date are not established.

subject: Animation — Vintage Banned Cartoons
verifiedFacts: Animation censorship has involved changing standards, distribution decisions, and the withdrawal or alteration of individual works.
The Censored Eleven are a documented group of Warner Bros. shorts withdrawn from United Artists syndication in 1968 for racist portrayals.
A generic compilation label cannot identify which titles are present.
interestingAngle: The honest story is about the danger of the label itself: a compilation called banned is an invitation to investigate, not permission to invent a censorship history.
doNotClaim: Individual cartoon titles, studios, dates, censorship reasons, and compilation source remain unknown.
No cultural controversy is attributed to the sampled frame.

subject: Paul Simon — You Can Call Me Al
editorialSubject: Paul Simon — You Can Call Me Al
verifiedFacts: The song was recorded at The Hit Factory in New York in April 1986 and released on Graceland.
The replacement video was directed by Gary Weis; Chevy Chase lip-syncs Simon’s lead vocal while Simon performs the backing-vocal joke.
The song eventually reached number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 after an earlier, lower entry and later resurgence.
interestingAngle: The video is a deliberately engineered misidentification machine: it makes the wrong person look like the singer, then keeps revealing the machinery as a joke.

used: canonical song identity, Graceland album, 1986 year, Billboard peak context
